items.title: Preparing for the interview
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles guidance; GOV.UK
items.body: When you are invited to interview, reply to confirm and read the invitation carefully for the date, time, format (often video), who the panel is and any adjustments on offer. Re-read the advert and list the behaviours and strengths it says will be assessed. For each behaviour prepare one or two real examples in STAR form, and write bullet notes, not scripts. Learn what the department and team do and why the job matters, so you can say why you want it. Do a trial run of the video call, in a quiet space, with childcare and interruptions arranged in advance. Have your ID ready if asked. Check whether notes are allowed in the room.

questions.prompt: What should you do first when you receive an interview invitation?

options.text: Ignore it until the day before
Ask for the questions in advance
Cancel it if you feel nervous
Confirm you can attend and read the details carefully

questions.prompt: How should you prepare examples for a behaviour-based interview?

options.text: Prepare several different real examples in STAR form that match the behaviours in the advert
Prepare one example and use it for every question
Memorise a word-for-word script
Do not prepare at all

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to research the department and the team before an interview?

options.text: It guarantees a job offer
To show you understand the work and why you want the job
It lets you skip the behaviour questions
Panels give marks for the number of facts you recite

questions.prompt: Your interview will be by video from home, and you have two young children. How do you prepare the day before and on the day?
questions.answer: The day before: test the link, camera, sound and internet, choose a quiet room with a plain background, arrange childcare or a partner to look after the children for the whole slot plus extra time, have ID, the invitation, a glass of water and STAR notes (if notes are allowed) ready. On the day: join a few minutes early, silence phones and notifications, and have a back-up plan such as a phone number for the panel if the link fails. If you need an adjustment, ask the recruitment team beforehand.
questions.rubric: Should cover testing technology, quiet space, childcare cover, documents, early join, a back-up plan and asking for adjustments if needed.

items.title: During the interview
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles guidance; GOV.UK
items.body: Most Civil Service interviews are held by a small panel, usually two or three people, who ask the same questions of every candidate so the process is fair. One person leads and the others take notes. Listen to the whole question and take a moment to think. If a question is unclear, ask politely for it to be repeated or explained. Answer with a specific example and use 'I'. Aim for answers of a couple of minutes, not one sentence and not ten minutes. It is fine to say 'Could I take a moment to think?' If you realise part-way that your example does not fit, say so and move to a better one. At the end you will usually be able to ask a question, so prepare one about the team or the job.

questions.prompt: Who usually interviews you for a Civil Service role?

options.text: Only the minister
A single person chosen at random
A small panel, often two or three people
The whole department

questions.prompt: A question is not clear to you. What is the best response?

options.text: Guess what is meant and answer anyway
Stay silent until they move on
Answer a different question you prefer
Politely ask for the question to be repeated or explained

questions.prompt: You cannot think of an example straight away. What is the best response?

options.text: Say you would like a moment to think, then answer
Make up an example
Say you have never done anything relevant
Change the subject

questions.prompt: You are asked: 'Tell us about a time when you disagreed with someone.' Plan your answer using STAR.
questions.answer: A good plan: Situation: a brief example, such as disagreeing with another parent on a school committee about how to spend funds. Task: I needed to reach a decision we could both support without damaging the working relationship. Action: I listened to their reasons, set out mine with the figures, suggested a compromise (split the money between both ideas) and checked they were comfortable. Result: we agreed, the event went ahead and we worked well together afterwards. The answer stays calm and fair, shows listening and compromise (Working Together, Communicating and Influencing) and uses 'I'.
questions.rubric: Should use all four STAR parts with a believable example, show listening and compromise, avoid blaming the other person, and have a clear result.

items.title: Strengths-based questions
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles guidance; GOV.UK
items.body: Strengths-based questions ask what you enjoy and what you do well. For example, 'What do you do when you are under pressure?' or 'What gives you the most energy?' They are often asked quickly, with short answers expected. There is no single right answer. The panel watches for energy, natural enthusiasm and honesty. Over-rehearsed answers sound false, so do not memorise lines. Before the interview, think about your own strengths: what people thank you for, what you find easy and enjoyable, what you lose track of time doing. Match these honestly to the role. If a role is mostly detailed administration and you hate detail, it is useful to know that before applying.

questions.prompt: What are strengths-based interview questions mostly about?

options.text: Only your qualifications
What you do well and enjoy
Only your past mistakes
Only your health

questions.prompt: Why is over-rehearsing a poor approach for strengths-based questions?

options.text: Rehearsing is forbidden
Panels do not score strengths
They test what comes naturally, so scripted answers can sound false
The questions are always the same

questions.prompt: What is a good approach to the question 'What activities give you energy?'

options.text: Say whatever you think the panel wants to hear
Say you have no preferences
Answer in one word
Answer honestly and give a real example of when you did the activity

questions.prompt: Identify three strengths you think you have and, for each, say how you know and how it would help in an administrative role.
questions.answer: A good answer names three genuine strengths with evidence, for example: organising, shown by coordinating a family and a community rota without missed shifts, which helps with managing caseloads and deadlines; listening, shown by friends and neighbours coming to me when they are stressed, which helps with customers who are upset; accuracy, shown by managing the household accounts to the penny, which helps with processing and checking. Each strength links to the role and is backed by a real example.
questions.rubric: Should name three honest strengths, give real evidence for each and link each to the administrative role.

items.title: After the interview
items.body: After the interview the panel scores each candidate against the criteria and the recruiting team makes decisions. You will be told the result and, if you are unsuccessful, you can ask for feedback, which is one of the most useful things you can get. If you pass but there are more successful candidates than vacancies, you may be placed on a reserve list, and offered a similar job if one comes up within a set period. A successful candidate receives a conditional offer, which is subject to the pre-employment checks. Being turned down is common and does not mean you are unsuitable: each application builds your skill and your examples. Use feedback, practise and apply again.

questions.prompt: If you are unsuccessful after an interview, what can you usually do?

options.text: Ask for feedback
Demand the job
Take legal action at once
Apply for the same job a second time the same day

questions.prompt: What is the most constructive step after an unsuccessful application?

options.text: Give up on the Civil Service
Use the feedback, improve your examples and apply for other roles
Argue with the panel
Stop practising

questions.prompt: What can being placed on a reserve list mean?

options.text: You have been rejected
You have already started work
You may be offered a similar job later if a vacancy comes up within a set period
You must retake all the tests

questions.prompt: You were unsuccessful at interview for an Administrative Officer role. Plan your next four weeks.
questions.answer: Week 1: ask for written feedback, read it, and write down what went well and what to improve. Week 2: update the STAR examples using the feedback and practise out loud with a friend. Week 3: practise tests (numerical, verbal, judgement) and check Civil Service Jobs alerts for new roles in your area. Week 4: apply for at least one or two new roles well before the closing dates. Keep a record of each application, and look after your confidence by noting what you have already achieved.
questions.rubric: Should include asking for feedback, improving examples, practice, new applications and keeping records or confidence. Should be a realistic weekly plan.
